answers.brief_reasoning: If Y picks high fare, X gets 100 with low fare and 73 with high fare. If Y picks low fare, X gets 51 with low fare and 36 with high fare. Low fare pays more either way.
answers.final_answer: Yes. Low fare is Airline X's dominant strategy: 100 > 73 when Y picks high fare, and 51 > 36 when Y picks low fare.

answers.brief_reasoning: The game is symmetric, so low fare is also dominant for Airline Y. Both firms playing their dominant strategy gives the equilibrium.
answers.final_answer: Airline X: low fare, Airline Y: low fare

answers.brief_reasoning: This is a prisoner's dilemma: each firm gains by cheating on the high-fare outcome.
answers.final_answer: Each firm has an incentive to cheat. If the other firm sets a high fare, a firm earns $100M by switching to a low fare instead of $73M by keeping a high fare. Low fare is dominant for both, and without an enforceable agreement neither can trust the other to keep a high fare. So both choose low fare and end up at ($51M, $51M).

answers.brief_reasoning: If Y charges a high fare, X can earn 61 by switching to a low fare instead of 49. Low fare is dominant for X, so any promise to keep fares high is not credible. Y expects X to cut its fare, and if X cuts it, Y does better with a low fare (43 > 35). Without an enforceable agreement, the firms end up at low fare, low fare.
answers.final_answer: Airline X has an incentive to cheat on a high-fare deal, earning 61 instead of 49 by charging a low fare. Low fare is X's dominant strategy, so its promise to keep fares high isn't credible. Y expects X to cut its fare and responds with a low fare, so the firms end up at the Nash equilibrium.
